chapter_theme: The greatness of those who have renounced: immeasurable, grounded in mastery of the senses, and shown in the force of their word and anger. It ends by saying that the name அந்தணர் belongs to those whose conduct is cool grace toward all beings.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: their greatness exceeds all others (21-23), its causes are quenching the five, yoga and knowledge of the principles (24-27), their authority (28-29), and their grace despite that authority (30).

21.reading: The settled view of the texts is to place the greatness of those who renounce within their discipline above all other excellence.
21.nuance: The verse says only ஒழுக்கத்து, in discipline. Parimelazhagar's ladder from duties of varna to release is his own construction. The commentators also give very different reasons for the agreement among texts.

positions.position: This is a shared conclusion of all religious texts, though they conflict on everything else.
positions.quote: ஒன்றையொன்று ஒவ்வாத சமய நூல்கள் எல்லாவற்றிற்கும் இஃது ஒத்த துணிவு

positions.position: Even a false text praises renunciants, so that people will honour it.

22.reading: Trying to state the measure of renouncers' greatness is like counting all the dead who have ever lived.
22.nuance: It's a strange image of praise. The dead aren't only numerous but past counting in principle. My reading, offered tentatively, is that comparing renouncers to the dead also suits people who have left the world.

23.reading: The greatness of those who discern the two ways and take on virtue here stands highest in the world.
23.nuance: ஈண்டு, here, is important: this choice is made in this life. Parimelazhagar uses an implied 'only' to place them above even emperors.

positions.position: The two are birth and release, weighed for their suffering and joy, and the virtue taken up is renunciation.
positions.quote: பிறப்பு வீடு என்னும் இரண்டனது துன்ப இன்பக் கூறுபாடுகளை ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து

positions.position: The two are good and evil, and anyone who chooses the good is great.

24.reading: One who guards the five with the goad of firmness is a seed for the finest ground.
24.nuance: The goad implies the elephants, which the verse doesn't mention, and then the image shifts to farming. வரன் leaves the 'field' open: Parimelazhagar makes it release, while Kalaignar makes it renunciation itself. The word உரன் suggests strength, though Parimelazhagar says it refers here to understanding.

25.reading: Of the strength of one who has quenched the five, Indra, lord of the wide heavens, is witness enough.
25.nuance: The verse does not say how Indra testifies. The commentators supply two opposed stories, one in which Indra failed and another in which he fears.

positions.position: Indra, cursed for failing to quench the five, shows by his own failure what the power is worth.
positions.quote: தான் ஐந்து அவியாது சாபம் எய்தி நின்று, அவித்தவனது ஆற்றல் உணர்த்தினான்

positions.position: Indra trembles for his throne when anyone does great penance, so the ascetic is stronger than the gods.

26.reading: Those who do what is hard to do are great, and those who can't do it are small.
26.nuance: The verse doesn't say what is hard, so it reads as general. In its context the commentators narrow it to yoga. Manakkudavar turns it into a warning within the chapter: renouncing alone does not make one great.

positions.position: What is hard is the eight limbs of yoga; what is easy is following the senses.
positions.quote: செயற்கு அரிய ஆவன, இமயம், நியமம் முதலாய எண்வகை யோக உறுப்புக்கள்.

positions.position: Those who have renounced are still small if they can't do these hard things.

27.reading: The world lies within the one who discerns the kinds of the five: taste, light, touch, sound and smell.
27.nuance: கட்டே is the crux. Pope's 'owns his sway' and Parimelazhagar's 'within his knowledge' suggest different kinds of mastery. Parimelazhagar's whole twenty-five principles are not in the couplet, which names only the five.

positions.position: This is knowledge of the twenty-five principles of Samkhya, beyond which there is no world.
This is the ability to understand and master the senses, which the world honours.

28.reading: The greatness of those whose word is full is shown on earth by their hidden words.
28.nuance: நிறைமொழி and மறைமொழி echo each other: a complete word and a concealed one. The verse doesn't say whether the proof is what the words do or what they teach.

positions.position: Renunciants' words take effect, and their commanding mantras prove it visibly.
positions.quote: அவர் ஆணையாகச் சொல்லிய மந்திரங்களே கண்கூடாகக் காட்டும்.

positions.position: 'Full' describes people of complete learning, whose mantras circulate as proof.
The proof is the enduring ethical books of the worthy.

29.reading: The anger of those who have climbed the hill of good qualities, even for a moment, is hard to withstand.
29.nuance: The crux is whose capacity காத்தல் refers to, and the commentators turn the verse in opposite directions. Pope sides with the threatening reading.

positions.position: Their anger lasts only a moment, yet its target cannot ward it off.
positions.quote: தான் உள்ள அளவு கணமே ஆயினும், வெகுளப்பட்டாரால் தடுத்தல் அரிது.

positions.position: The harm from their anger can't be avoided, as in Nahusha's becoming a serpent.
Such people can't hold on to anger, even for a moment.

30.reading: Those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, because they live clothed in cool kindness toward every living being.
30.nuance: The verse defines a status word by conduct, and its logic is a reason (ஒழுகலான்), so the name follows from the behaviour. Placed right after 29, its coolness is the counterweight to the sage's terrifying anger.

positions.position: The name's reason restricts it to those with such grace, namely those in renunciation.
Having said some renunciants are small, the verse says some non-renunciants are great.
Any worthy person with love for all beings is an அந்தணர்.

links.note: Here the texts' settled view exalts renouncers above all. In 49, on Parimelazhagar's reading, the thing called virtue is household life, and renunciation is good only if it is blameless. The book states both verdicts without reconciling them.
Both define greatness by rare, difficult acts. Chapter 3 says this of renouncers, while 975 in the chapter on greatness says it of the great in general, so the test is not limited to ascetics.

Here the sage's unstoppable anger shows his stature. In 301, real restraint means holding anger back exactly where it can hurt. By the standard of 301, the anger praised in 29 is what should be held back.
Both make conduct the test of priestly status: 30 defines அந்தணர் by compassion, and 134 says a பார்ப்பான் is lost if conduct fails, even though forgotten scripture can be relearned.

source_issues: Manakkudavar is not aligned for verse 27. His comment on verse 30 says 'these eight', which suggests his grouping of this chapter differs from the running order here.
